overview: Many canals built by the Bureau of Reclamation, the Interior Department agency that runs federal water projects in the West, are now operated by local water districts, and some of them run through cities and neighborhoods. This bill creates a category called an 'urban canal of concern': a canal stretch the Interior Department classifies as urban and whose failure would put more than 100 people at risk. It lets the department or the local operator carry out major repair and rehabilitation work on these canals. For non-emergency work, the federal government would pay 25 percent of the cost outright, and would advance the rest as a loan that the local water district repays. As of September 17, 2026, a Senate committee had approved it with changes and it was placed on the Senate calendar for possible floor action.
for: Supporters say aging canals that now run through populated areas pose real flood risks to nearby residents, and sharing repair costs helps local districts fix them before they fail.
against: Critics say the bill shifts part of the cost of maintaining locally operated canals onto federal taxpayers, and that districts benefiting from the water should bear the full cost of upkeep.
